title: Carcass or temple: what the body is
claim: The Naladiyar mostly treats the body as a pot seeping filth from nine openings, a stinking cart for vultures, and a skin bag the dancer leaves behind; seeing it so is meant to cool desire and turn one to renunciation. The Tirumanthiram holds that view and its opposite side by side. Its chapter on the body's impermanence (யாக்கை நிலையாமை) speaks in the Naladiyar's voice, almost in its words (167 against Naladiyar 26), while the teaching chapter just before it makes the body the temple where Nandi dwells (116). Later tantras build on the temple: the body of flesh is the Lord's shrine (1823), its very form is the Sivalinga and the dance (1726), and those who dismiss it as filth are dull (2137). In 725 Tirumular tells the change as his own: he once held the body base, then saw that the Highest had made it his temple, and now he tends it. He does not drop the older view: to the unreleased the body is still a prison (1701), and only a jnani's corpse is exempt from the Naladiyar's indifference to the dead body (1910, 1911). Even the Naladiyar values the body as a means: it is rare to obtain and its fruit should be taken (34), as Tirumular nourishes it because without it one cannot attain true knowledge (724).
limits: The Naladiyar's body verses mostly serve to cure lust, so each tension holds only if they are read as a verdict on the body itself. 725's 'once' is a turn in the speaker's understanding, not a sign that the tantras are in the order he wrote them, and whether the Naladiyar or the Tirumanthiram borrowed the dancer-in-the-bag verse is not known.
audit_issue: Counter-evidence: in 2137's own chapter, 2125 lists the body's fluids, flesh, fat, bone and marrow as a perishing adjunct much as Naladiyar 46 does, and 2122 repeats the bag left by a departing thief. 724 and Naladiyar 34 share an instrumental valuation more than they clash.
audit_corrections: Claim corrected after the audit for the errors it found (verse positions, 724's wording, the 'one verb' framing); the corrected text was not re-audited.

title: Leaping past Death
claim: The Kural says the power won by austerity can even leap past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தல், 269); the Naladiyar answers with the same verb that no one here has leapt past Death and escaped, so give your wealth now (6), and that grey hair will surely come (11). The Tirumanthiram holds both views. Several first-tantra verses side with the Naladiyar: Death does not ask whether one is young (255), black hair turns white (192), and a man can die between supper and bed (148, with Kural 336); a verse in the third tantra adds that all who came before have ended (596). The third tantra's yoga sides with the Kural and goes further: those who know the way have no Yama (711), Death's word does not reach the yogi even in dreams (622), and practice undoes grey hair and wrinkles (647, 848, 727). Only once does Tirumular use the disputed verb itself, in the first tantra and against the Naladiyar's use of it: shed your wealth and you may leap past Death (172).
limits: Every tension holds only on a literal reading of Tirumular's promises. Tradition also reads them as freedom from fear of death or from Yama's judgement after death, and on that reading the books need not clash. Kural 269 is itself read literally by Parimelazhagar and figuratively by Kalaignar.
audit_issue: The first-tantra/third-tantra split is loose: 176, in the first tantra's chapter on wealth, already says Yama's messengers do not come near those who think of the Lord. 622 reads more naturally as freedom from Death's threat than as bodily escape, and 192's last line is too obscure to make greying a stated warning.
audit_corrections: Claim corrected after the audit for the errors it found (verse positions, 724's wording, the 'one verb' framing); the corrected text was not re-audited.
